profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a small civic-tech nonprofit building a volunteer-run web platform called BlockFix, which lets residents report neighborhood issues like broken streetlights and illegal dumping to city departments and track follow-up. The team is preparing the next six-week milestone before a public demo to neighborhood organizers and a check-in with the city innovation office. The specific planning task is to decide what will be included in the milestone around a new 'community triage' workflow, how the work will be split between product and engineering, and what timeline they will commit to. The agenda is to align on the milestone scope, define what a 'pilot-ready' release means, assign ownership for setup and rollout tasks, and confirm the date of the internal handoff before the public demo. The expected outcome is a shared-seeming implementation plan for shipping the triage workflow, onboarding a small set of neighborhoods, and preparing a demoable release.

members.name: Maya Chen
members.expertise: Civic-tech product planning, volunteer coordination, community research, pilot design
members.background: Maya came from a community organizing nonprofit and now runs product for the BlockFix project, translating organizer needs into lightweight software plans and keeping external partners engaged despite a part-time volunteer engineering team.
members.private_state: She wants a milestone plan that looks dependable to community partners and the city office, while keeping commitments small enough that the volunteer team can realistically ship something demoable; she is especially concerned about not overloading organizers with setup work before the demo.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a feature is 'pilot-ready,' it means residents and organizers in two selected neighborhoods can use it end-to-end with real issue reports, even if some admin work is still manual behind the scenes.
The 'beta neighborhoods' already refers to the two organizer groups from South Park and River East that she has been speaking with for weeks, so rollout planning can presume those partners.

Asking engineering to 'set up the pilot' includes preloading the neighborhood categories, volunteer routing rules, and a basic intake form configuration because those are part of making the workflow usable.
An internal handoff date of 'next Friday' means by end of day in her local time so she can review on Monday and circulate demo materials early the next week.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Full-stack web engineering, deployment automation, open-source infrastructure, lightweight moderation tools
members.background: Leo is a senior engineer who joined from a municipal SaaS vendor and now leads a small group of volunteer developers, focusing on maintainable releases and minimizing custom one-off configuration that the team cannot support long term.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the team from hidden operational work and avoid promising production-grade community onboarding before the architecture is stable; he is mainly concerned about getting a technically clean release that volunteers can maintain after the demo.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says a feature is 'pilot-ready,' it means the triage workflow is deployed in staging-like production infrastructure, tested by the team, and safe to show, but not necessarily populated with live neighborhood-specific content or external users yet.
The phrase 'beta neighborhoods' refers to the generic neighborhood fixtures in the seed dataset used in prior demos, not any externally committed organizer groups.
Engineering 'setup' for the pilot means enabling the feature flag, deploying the release, and documenting the admin screens so product or organizers can enter local routing information themselves.
A deadline of 'next Friday' means before the nightly deployment window closes in UTC, since that is how he thinks about release cutoffs and volunteer availability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need the triage workflow to be 'pilot-ready' for the milestone.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means ready for limited real-world use by actual organizers and residents in two neighborhoods, with any missing back-office steps handled manually if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means ready for a stable team-run release that can be demonstrated and internally exercised, without assuming real external users or neighborhood-specific operational readiness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software planning, 'pilot-ready' sounds like a normal shared milestone label, and both interpretations plausibly fit a pre-demo release, so each hears confirmation of their own standard without suspecting a gap.

misalignment_points.topic: Which neighborhoods are in the beta
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss rolling the workflow out to the 'beta neighborhoods.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya is thinking specifically of South Park and River East, the two community groups she has been informally preparing for launch.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is thinking of the existing demo neighborhood records in the seeded environment that engineering informally calls the beta neighborhoods.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have repeatedly heard the phrase 'beta neighborhoods' in project updates, and the term sounds concrete enough that neither thinks to restate the exact names because they assume the reference is already common ground.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that engineering will 'handle setup' before the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya includes configuring neighborhood-specific categories, routing rules, and default moderation settings so organizers can start using the workflow immediately.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo limits setup to code deployment, feature-flag activation, and making the configuration UI available, leaving local content entry and routing configuration to product or partner admins.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Setup is treated as background implementation work rather than a headline planning item, so the phrase feels administrative and not worth unpacking, even though each side silently includes different boundary lines.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both commit to having it 'ready by next Friday' for the internal handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya believes 'ready' means a reviewable build with the pilot neighborhoods configured and stable enough for her to run through the full organizer flow before the weekend.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo believes 'ready' means the code branch is merged and deployed by the Friday UTC release window, with configuration and partner-specific checks able to happen afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline talk in planning meetings often compresses multiple completion criteria into a single date phrase, and both assume their notion of what counts as done is the obvious one attached to the deadline.

turns.inner_thought: I need this milestone framed around something I can confidently describe to the organizers and the city office. For me, pilot-ready means South Park and River East can actually submit real reports through the triage flow end-to-end, even if we do some manual cleanup behind the curtain. The volunteer engineers cannot carry a huge scope, so I should keep the language crisp and practical.
turns.utterance: I want to center this six-week milestone on getting the community triage flow pilot-ready before the organizer demo and the city check-in. If we can leave this cycle with that in place, I think the rest of the story gets much easier.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds achievable if we keep Maya from turning this into a full onboarding push. Pilot-ready, to me, is a clean release on stable infrastructure that our team can exercise and safely show, not full external operational readiness. I need to steer toward a narrow core workflow and avoid hidden support work.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I think we can get it pilot-ready in that window if we keep the release surface narrow and stay focused on the core triage path. I'd rather make that solid than spread the team across a bunch of edge workflow pieces.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he is aligned. The point is to have the two organizer groups I've been talking with actually using the flow soon after the demo so we can gather grounded feedback instead of hypothetical reactions. I should keep saying beta neighborhoods since that is the shared term everyone has been using.
turns.utterance: Right, and the main outcome I'm aiming for is that the beta neighborhoods are using the flow so we can collect concrete feedback right after the demo instead of just general impressions. That feels important for both the partners and the city conversation.

turns.inner_thought: That part should be straightforward because the seeded demo neighborhoods already exist in the environment. If we're just wiring the new workflow into those records, we avoid extra one-off data prep. Sounds like Maya is talking about the same beta neighborhoods we always use internally.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. The beta neighborhoods are already in the seeded environment, so from our side it's mostly a matter of wiring the new workflow in and making sure the core path behaves the way we expect.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Then engineering can take care of the pieces that make those neighborhoods actually usable: categories, routing rules, moderation defaults, intake basics. I really do not want organizers spending the milestone clicking through admin fields just to get to a demoable flow.
turns.utterance: Given that, I'd really like engineering to handle setup before the handoff. I don't want the organizers carrying extra admin work during the milestone if we can avoid it.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree to handle setup as long as that means deployment, feature flagging, and exposing the admin screens. I definitely do not want engineering owning all neighborhood-specific configuration forever. If the UI is there, product or partner admins can tweak whatever they need.
turns.utterance: Yeah, we can handle setup on the engineering side. Once the flag is on, the admin screens should let the neighborhood teams make any small adjustments themselves without needing us in the loop for every little change.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure South Park's requested issue buckets are covered, but I don't want to turn this into a debate about ownership. That should just be part of setup for the beta rollout, same as the other neighborhood-specific pieces. If he agrees generally, I can keep the organizers shielded from the work.
turns.utterance: Okay, that makes sense. One thing I do want to make sure fits naturally into the setup for the beta rollout is that the issue buckets we've been hearing about can slot in cleanly, because that's likely to come up quickly once people start using it.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds like content entry after deployment, not something engineering should hard-code into the milestone. I should acknowledge it without expanding scope. The real risk area is whether triage transitions and audit trails are reliable enough for a maintainable release.
turns.utterance: I think that should be manageable as a small adjustment after deployment. The bigger thing I want to protect time for is making sure the triage states and the audit logging are stable, because that's what will make the workflow feel trustworthy.

turns.inner_thought: I need a usable build in my hands by end of day next Friday, local time, with the pilot neighborhoods configured so I can test the full organizer flow over the weekend and prepare materials on Monday. I'll phrase it as the internal handoff since that should be obvious.
turns.utterance: Can we have everything ready by next Friday for the internal handoff? I'd like enough time right after that to go through it and get the partner-facing materials lined up.

turns.inner_thought: Next Friday works if we aim for the normal UTC evening deployment cutoff. That means code merged, released, and stable enough for internal review; any local configuration can happen after. I should keep expectations on polish contained so the volunteers aren't scrambling.
turns.utterance: Next Friday is workable from my side if we target the usual evening release window and keep the final polish limited. That gives us a clean cutoff for the volunteers and a predictable handoff.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I can keep South Park and River East warm without overcommitting details. Once engineering finishes setup, I should be able to run through submission, triage, and organizer review myself over the weekend before sharing anything outward.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll take the follow-up with the neighborhood contacts, and once setup is done I'll run through the organizer flow over the weekend so we can catch anything awkward before we put it in front of partners.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this sounds contained: we ship the triage workflow, do setup in the engineering sense, and hit the Friday release cutoff. Maya can handle whatever partner-specific tweaks or walkthroughs come after that. I think we have a reasonable milestone now.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. So engineering owns shipping the triage workflow, handling setup, and having it ready by next Friday, and then we can use the following days for your walkthrough and any light follow-up.
